title: Early Scottish records
standfirst: The early Scottish records anchor the search for one extended Glasgow family. The next task is to connect its oldest documented households, retaining tentative joins with their evidence and open questions.
question: How can the earliest Glasgow branches be joined into the shared paternal family?
answer: Start with the 1447–1455 Glasgow burgess, the Stirling John of 1475–1480, Alan in the late-fifteenth-century justice record, and the Saltmarket family. The Saltmarket John-to-William property succession is the leading father hypothesis, followed by a proved father–son generation. These working connections guide a single-family reconstruction while the missing identities and generations are tested.

chapters.title: Connect the oldest families
body: The ancestry programme now measures separate paternal components, unattached fathers with at least two children, the largest branch and connected pairs. Confidently marked and working links are reported separately, with a fixed initial cohort for progress comparisons.

Prioritise the oldest unresolved connection and extend it to supported siblings. Use post-1850 evidence when it can resolve an earlier branch, rather than making later descendant reconstruction the main work.

evidence.label: Ancestry progress, family heads and earliest connection tests

chapters.title: Medieval and early-burgh occurrences
body: Medieval officeholders, messengers, clerics and burgh entries preserve name occurrences across several places and roles.
A shared surname, an office phrase or a similar John does not itself establish one person or a descent line; pre-1500 subjects remain documentary research destinations.

The official description of the 8 August 1475 Stirling charter, B66/25/43, groups John Glesgw among the burgess witnesses. Three Stirling occurrences are now assigned to the same working identity. This strengthens the civic comparison with the Glasgow burgess of 1447–1455; one career across 1447–1480 is viable, and an estimated circa-1450 birth cannot establish a separate son. Parent–child or other kinship remains an alternative. Saltmarket activity is secure in 1527; the 1506 alias-Smith identification remains possible.

evidence.label: John of Stirling: three source-described acts and identity alternatives

chapters.title: Glasgow property and craft records
body: Protocols, burgess admissions and testaments permit especially careful reconstruction in the Glasgow burgh, including one expressly named parent–child generation.
The Saltmarket succession and fisher household have different evidential strengths; their surrounding probable relationships remain labelled rather than silently converted into descent.

chapters.title: Ayrshire estates, households and ministry
body: Teind lists, charters, sasines and parish material document people at Corsankell, Stevenston, Kilwinning and Kilbirnie.
Some records explicitly define a household; estate proximity, later local tradition and same-name candidates remain research leads until a record states the bridge.

chapters.title: Calder and Lothian testaments and registers
body: Testaments at Hirmenschelis and Corstoun name small households, while baptism indexes provide two sequences for a father called James Glasgow.
The records correct earlier inherited claims, but they do not identify every child with a modern profile or settle whether the James sequences represent one household.

chapters.title: Findmypast follow-up: indexed records and open originals (15 October 2026)
body: The focused follow-up authenticated William Glascoe's 10 July 1610 South Leith marriage to Catherine Fraith/Fraser and records a new Haddington household: Issobell Glasgow, born 24 and baptised 26 November 1639, daughter of William Glasgow and Issobella Miral.

Crossle's 9 December 1639 abstract names an Archbold Glascow clerk; the duplicate transcript IDs are retained, but the original document 849 has not been inspected, so identification with Archibald Glasgow-1101 remains probable. Walter's 1647/1649 and Margaret's 1649/1646 competing indexes require original-page checks.

Visually checked SRO Indexes 38 pp.187–188 name Alexander as son of James, the Fisherrow tailor and Musselburgh burgess; Christina Bye is James’s spouse and Janet Clerk is Alexander’s. Indexes 44 pp.159–160 repeatedly associate Alexander with James, weaver: 14 February 1646 (33/258), 15 May 1646 (33/360), 10 February 1647 (34/287). Edward shares the first 1646 reference. The earlier June 1646 attribution belongs to Isobel Givan in the preceding row. These are registration dates; original instruments remain unread.

James the weaver could be the older James, Alexander’s son James-3923, the Edinburgh weaver James-1150, or another man. Eduard-994, indexed in Inveresk in 1609 with father James, is an alternative to Edwards 1557 and 1558. A match could explain the association within the proposed Fisherrow household. The possible Corsankell bridge and exact kinship remain open; this batch adds no paternal join.
The 1623 Robert Glasgow tanner and 1625 town-officer references remain separate identity questions.

clusters.title: Medieval and early-burgh occurrences
clusters.summary: Entries establish recorded bearers and roles in multiple places before a continuous pedigree can be demonstrated.
clusters.boundary: They do not establish a shared medieval founder or identify same-named people across records.

clusters.title: Glasgow burgh property and fishers
clusters.summary: Property records directly identify some parent–child links and testaments define a fisher family core.
clusters.boundary: The older title succession and unresolved John identities do not prove every attached descendant.

clusters.title: Ayrshire estate and parish records
clusters.summary: Tenancy, charter and church sources preserve households and careers in the Ayrshire corridor.
clusters.boundary: Neighbourhood, later tradition and a common surname do not supply the missing connections.

clusters.title: Calder and Lothian testament and register records
clusters.place: Calder district, Mid Calder and Inveresk
clusters.summary: Two testaments identify separate rural households; baptism indexes frame a carefully bounded James question.
clusters.boundary: Neither testament proves a burgh bridge or resolves all later-profile identities.

links.label: same-name and title questions require explicit documentary bridges
property and associate evidence offers leads, not a proved route

proved: specific named relationships and events within individual records
record-defined household groups where a source states the relationship
hypothesis: bridges between burgh, Ayrshire and other local clusters
unresolved: a complete early Scottish pedigree and common medieval origin

gaps.title: Read original property and estate instruments
gaps.why: Heir, widow, witness and holding clauses can provide the explicit bridge that indexes and abstracts lack.

gaps.title: Verify original parish pages
gaps.why: Witnesses, occupations and residences may distinguish same-named households.

gaps.title: Resolve the associated Huchesoun fragment
gaps.why: Its archival boundary must be understood before it can be used as a family-network lead.

gaps.title: Keep documentary subjects separate from profile identities
gaps.why: A matching name or chronology alone should not create or join a person profile.
